extracted.intended_audience: business leaders, communications teams, crisis managers, and PR professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Practical best-practice guidance and lessons learned for organizational crisis management and crisis communications, illustrated with real-world case studies across industries. Focuses on planning, team structure, response actions, messaging, reputation protection, and post-crisis learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proactive planning, transparency, and agility
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective crisis management occurs when an organization employs skillful planning and a proactive response to avert a crisis entirely, limit its severity and duration, or turn it into an opportunity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize transparency and agility as core objectives; anticipate likely threats and develop strategies to cope with their impact; use planning to avert or reduce crises and to pivot quickly when circumstances change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form a crisis team
rubrics_metrics.description: Have a designated crisis management team, and smaller cross-functional teams for specific issues when needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include representatives from communications, technical, legal, and other relevant functions; free team members from normal duties, remove constraints, give them resources (including external experts), and review the team's performance after the crisis. (Example: Volkswagen task force with 24/7 work.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a crisis plan (including communications and social media)
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain a detailed crisis management plan that includes a communications plan and social media contingencies; if missing, do rapid initial planning at crisis onset.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft holding statements in advance, plan for social media channels, use templates and step-by-step guides, and prepare rapid-response materials. (Negative example: Amazon appeared to lack a plan during Prime Day protests.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick the right spokesperson
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose an individual with knowledge, training, and position of authority to address the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coach the spokesperson in media handling but avoid putting an uninformed or low-authority representative in front of cameras (positive example: Dr. Anthony Fauci; guidance on reaching multiple media formats).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be present (leadership visibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should be visibly on site or at an appropriate location during serious crises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cancel trips and return from vacations when necessary; absence or secrecy about leaders' whereabouts can create scandal and distract from response (Scott Morrison example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond quickly (issue initial statement within the first hour)
rubrics_metrics.description: Issue a public statement rapidly—within the first hour if possible—and publish frequent updates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep stakeholders informed about progress; when uncertain, err on the side of too much communication rather than too little. (Positive example: KFC acknowledged and updated rapidly; negative: GM delayed/obfuscated and harmed reputation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be compassionate and empathetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond with empathy to show your organization cares about people affected by the crisis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance legal risk management with clear human concern; avoid legalistic, cold language that undermines trust (Boeing example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speak the truth and be transparent
rubrics_metrics.description: Be upfront, transparent, and avoid euphemisms or jargon; do not try to obscure facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The truth typically emerges; obfuscation breeds mistrust and worse consequences (United Airlines example where euphemistic language backfired).

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the crisis while aligning with long-term strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Give the crisis full attention but do not lose sight of the organization’s future and overarching goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, align response actions with long-term vision and use the recovery to rebuild stability (Delta example: retained CFO to help rebuild).

rubrics_metrics.name: Communicate clearly and simply
rubrics_metrics.description: Present information openly and in ways stakeholders can understand; recognize perspective differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid hiding bad news or relying on incomplete or misleading information; establish clear channels between engineers/practitioners and decision makers (Challenger example showed poor communication caused disaster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguard brand and reputation with authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Protect your reputation by conveying authenticity and empathy; reputation is a primary determiner of brand value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that reputation affects consumer behavior and financial outcomes; use apologies, authentic engagement, and long-term stewardship to protect brand value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast and decisive operational action (recalls, halting ads, stakeholder outreach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Take swift, concrete operational steps to protect people and limit harm, even if costly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include halting advertising, notifying stakeholders, establishing hotlines, and national recalls (Tylenol: recall costing >$100M but restored trust). Prioritize safety over short-term cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty and integrity in leadership messaging
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should not evade blame and should express genuine regret and responsibility when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candid leadership statements can preserve or rebuild trust (Tylenol CEO James Burke praised for honesty); insincere or defensive messaging damages credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for worst-case scenarios and rehearse procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate black-swan and high-impact events, and rehearse emergency procedures through drills and exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular exercises and clear emergency procedures help responders act effectively; absence of drills was a key failure in Bhopal and Katrina analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empower teams and encourage candor
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders should empower staff to innovate and solve problems, and encourage honest communication across levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flatten decision processes when needed, promote collaborative problem-solving with stakeholders, and provide staff support (Cleveland Clinic Abu Dhabi: cross-level team, staff care measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Decentralize decision-making to improve speed and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Move away from rigid hierarchical decision-making where necessary to improve responsiveness and ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enable collaboration with customers, suppliers, regulators, and competitors; support remote work cultures that prioritize trust and results (HBS study of Chinese executives during COVID).

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed lessons and innovations into organizational muscle memory
rubrics_metrics.description: Capture new learnings and digital or process innovations that arise during a crisis and institutionalize them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convert temporary fixes and cultural shifts into lasting practices so the organization is better prepared next time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation is key — maintain infrastructure, supplies, and evacuation plans
rubrics_metrics.description: Invest in correct engineering, preparedness funding, pre-positioned emergency supplies, and logistics for vulnerable populations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failures in infrastructure design, underfunding, or logistical planning (Katrina levees, lack of evacuation for people without cars) dramatically worsen outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train your crisis team and clarify roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure crisis response leaders have disaster management experience and that all agencies/teams know their roles and responsibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid political appointments without relevant expertise and conduct role-clarity exercises; FEMA/Katrina failures highlighted unclear responsibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplify communications and decision-making structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid overly complex, fragmented response plans with too many actors and incompatible systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit unnecessary bureaucracy, ensure compatible technology and clear escalation paths so that decision-making is not paralyzed (Katrina example with 29 federal agencies).

rubrics_metrics.name: Act quickly but not rashly (avoid wasteful or fraudulent spending)
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond rapidly but maintain basic controls to prevent waste, fraud, and misallocation of resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure procurement and distribution processes are controlled and purposeful; Katrina FEMA spending examples show how haste without planning creates other harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize crisis readiness and don't starve safety for cost savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Maintain training, staffing, safety mechanisms, and necessary supplies rather than cutting them to save costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cost-cutting that reduces safety (Bhopal, Takata) increases catastrophic risk; adequate staffing, testing, and safety systems are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share information promptly across units and with authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate internal findings and proprietary safety information to other sites and public health authorities when it affects public safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to share known risks (Bhopal example where U.S. plant's findings weren't shared) prevents responders from treating victims correctly and hampers mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and sustain a safety culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a corporate culture that prioritizes safety, encourages raising concerns, and avoids normalizing weak signals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid overconfidence and short-term profit pressures that lead to ignored warnings and suppressed alarms (BP, Takata). Implement independent reviews and maintenance regimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Live up to company values to avoid scandals
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure corporate incentives and management behavior align with stated values to prevent systemic abuses and scandals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aggressive sales targets or misaligned incentives (Wells Fargo) lead employees to commit misconduct; leadership must act to enforce values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take prevention and planning for cyber/data crises seriously
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement up-to-date patching, data governance, monitoring, and timely disclosure for cybersecurity incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Basic IT hygiene failures (expired certificates, unpatched servers, poor access controls) lead to massive breaches (Equifax); public disclosure timing and response UX matter a great deal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior leadership must maintain oversight of risk
rubrics_metrics.description: The C-suite must stay informed and scrutinize risky activities to prevent concealment and group-think.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure independent review teams and rigorous risk-management standards; concealment or changing metrics to hide problems (London Whale) magnifies damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apologize when you are wrong and do so in a timely manner
rubrics_metrics.description: If the organization is at fault, issue a sincere apology promptly rather than delaying or minimizing wrongdoing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delays or non-apologies (Facebook's delayed response) undermine recovery; apologies should be backed by corrective actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor and manage social media actively and appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuously monitor social media for emerging issues and respond quickly with appropriate tone—sometimes humor, sometimes solemnity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speed and tone are critical: cheeky, timely responses can defuse some issues (Popeye’s, Red Cross, Tide), while defensiveness, profanity, or deleting user posts (Tinder, Applebee’s) backfire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-crisis specific: take responsibility and implement fixes
rubrics_metrics.description: For product failures, show concern for customers, accept responsibility when appropriate, and enact decisive product safety improvements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actions can include recalls, supplier changes, enhanced QA, transparent investigations, and repeated apologies (Mattel, Samsung examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use crisis communications templates and holding statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage pre-built crisis communications strategy templates and holding statements to speed early-stage messaging and role assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Templates help assign responsibilities and build early process and response; Smartsheet and other resources provide step-by-step templates for rapid use.
